The ongoing global AI buildout keeps on squeezing the supply of consumer GPUs. Prices on graphics cards have gotten higher and higher throughout 2026, and industry leaders suggest that prices will only continue to rise. The 2026 Black Friday deals season may offer some relief if you need a new gaming GPU, at least versus current market pricing.

If you're in a position where you need to upgrade your GPU, or if you just want to get ahead of Grand Theft Auto VI 's eventual PC release, prices now are as low as you're likely to find, possibly for years going forward.

Finding a graphics card anywhere near MSRP is largely a thing of the distant past in late 2026. We're now looking for lows relative to highly elevated current prices. And even then, the price-to-performance ratio of some graphics cards is low enough that we wouldn't recommend them at all. If you're going to spend lots of money on a graphics upgrade, you want to be sure it'll last.

We select deals based on our in-depth knowledge, gained from thorough reviews, expansive benchmarks, and extensive historical price analysis, and then keep them listed here in this constantly updated article. We're seeing a lot better value on AMD and Intel cards than on Nvidia-powered offerings, but you can still find some savings on RTX cards.

The best deals on GPUs go out of stock quickly, as well. We're keeping this list updated around the clock with the latest prices, so check back regularly if you're shopping for a particular GPU.

To make sure you're spending your hard-earned cash wisely, make sure to check out our guide to the best graphics cards for gaming before jumping on any juicy-looking deal this Black Friday season.

Check out our list of the best graphics cards for targeted purchasing advice across a range of price points, and our GPU benchmark hierarchy to view evergreen performance data, regardless of sales trends.

What to Look for in a Black Friday Graphics Card Deal

When shopping for a graphics card, consider the following.

🔎 What resolution, settings do you want to play at? A low-end budget graphics card can play games at 1080p in medium settings, but if you want to play at ultra settings, you'll need to get at least a mid-range card. As you move up the stack of cards, you can play at 2K resolution and higher settings or, with the priciest cards, 4K.

🔎 How many FPS do you consider smooth? Most people consider 30 fps the bare minimum for playability and 60 fps decent. However, if you want less lag for eSports gaming, you'll want to be able to go to over 100 fps at reasonable settings. See our GPU benchmark hierarchy to find out how each GPU fares.

🔎 Do you have enough power? Make sure that you have enough capacity from your power supply to support the card. If you're not sure, use a tool such as Newegg's power supply calculator to see how much you need. If your power supply can't handle the card, either get a new PSU or a different card.

🔎 Will it fit in your case? If you've got a small PC case, make sure you check the length of the card against the case's clearance numbers.
